title: Chemistry IX · 2023 · E-Marking Notes (Questions & Solved Better Responses)
subject: Chemistry
introduction: This document has been produced for the teachers and candidates of Secondary School Certificate (SSC) Part I Chemistry. It contains official comments on candidates' responses to the 2023 SSC-I Examination indicating the quality of the responses and highlighting their relative strengths and weaknesses.
generalObservations: Most candidates achieved success in constructing good responses, particularly in the case of drawing atomic structure and determining the empirical formula and molecular formula of a compound. Nonetheless, it is essential for teachers to concentrate on electronic configurations with proper placement of subatomic particles, physical properties of elements across groups, kinetic molecular theory, balancing chemical equations, and differentiating electrolysis of aqueous brine from molten salt.

questions.questionText:
Draw the structure of an ion with the following features.
• Charge of −3
• Atomic number = 15
• Nucleon number = 31
questions.sloText: Draw the atomic structure of the first twenty elements of the periodic table and their ions using their mass number.
checkingHints: 1 mark for showing the correct number of shells with electrons (2, 8, 8).
1 mark for showing the nucleus with the correct number of neutrons (16) and protons (15).
1 mark for showing the charge on the ion (-3) outside brackets.
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates demonstrated a good understanding of ion formation, particularly for the features given in the question. They accurately depicted the ionic structure of P^3- ions showcasing a strong grasp of the concept. However, some candidates exhibited misconceptions with reference to differences in electron numbers after ion formation. To improve weaker responses, candidates should focus on understanding the concept of ions better and emphasise gaining electrons to form an ion rather than assuming equal numbers of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses showed clarity in illustrating the key components (electron, proton, neutron) with a -3 charge and correctly mentioned the proton number (15), number of electrons (18), valence electrons, and the electronic arrangement before and after ion formation.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses displayed some misconceptions regarding ions. While they attempted to draw the structure of P^3- ions, they showed a lack of understanding of the difference in electron numbers after ion formation. Many incorrectly assumed equal numbers of protons, neutrons, and electrons in the P^3- ion.
suggestions: Utilise interactive visual aids or simulations to help students visualise electron gain during anion formation.
Provide regular structured drills calculating protons (Z), neutrons (A - Z), and electrons (Z - charge) for both neutral atoms and polyvalent ions.
questions.modelAnswer:
Phosphide Ion (P^3-) Structure:
• Protons = 15
• Neutrons = 31 - 15 = 16
• Electrons = 15 + 3 = 18 electrons (Configuration: 2, 8, 8)
• Drawing features central nucleus labeled [15p, 16n] enclosed by 3 concentric electron rings (2 in K-shell, 8 in L-shell, 8 in M-shell) within square brackets with charge -3: [ :P: ]^3-

questions.sloText: Discuss the physical and chemical properties of: a. group I b. group II c. group VII d. group VIII.
checkingHints: 1 mark for odour of chlorine: pungent / choking / suffocating odour.
1 mark for physical state of bromine: liquid (at room temperature).
1 mark for colour of iodine: purple / violet / dark grey-black.
questions.overallPerformance: The overall performance of candidates in understanding the general physical properties of Halogens (Group VII A) was satisfactory. However, weaker responses demonstrated a lack of content knowledge, leading to difficulty in recognising these physical properties correctly.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses exhibited a strong content knowledge and understanding of the general properties of halogens. They accurately identified the pungent odour of chlorine, the liquid state of bromine at room temperature, and the purple/dark grey colour of iodine.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses struggled to recognise the physical properties of halogens. They often mistook the odour of chlorine for an odourless gas. Additionally, there were misconceptions about the physical state at room temperature and the colour of bromine and iodine respectively.
suggestions: Reinforce the physical states and colours of halogens down Group VII: Fluorine (pale yellow gas), Chlorine (greenish-yellow pungent gas), Bromine (reddish-brown volatile liquid), Iodine (lustrous dark purple-black solid).
Use mnemonic charts and lab demonstration videos of halogen physical specimens.
questions.modelAnswer:
• Chlorine (Cl) Odour = Pungent / choking odour
• Bromine (Br) Physical State at Room Temperature = Liquid
• Iodine (I) Colour = Purple / violet / dark grey-black

questions.questionText:
When ammonium chloride (NH4Cl) is heated in a test tube, it results in the formation of ammonia (NH3) and hydrogen chloride (HCl) gases. The fumes of the gases can be observed moving along the test tube.
(Note: Atomic mass of N = 14 amu, H = 1 amu and Cl = 35.5 amu)
a. Name the process that allows the movement of gases along the test tube. (1 Mark)
b. Which gas, ammonia or hydrogen chloride, will travel at a faster speed? Give a suitable reason to support your answer. (2 Marks)
questions.sloText: Explain the properties of gases: a. diffusion b. effusion c. condensation d. density e. compressibility.
checkingHints: 1 mark for naming diffusion.
1 mark for identifying ammonia (NH3).
1 mark for stating that rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to molecular mass (Graham's law) with correct molar masses: NH3 (17) vs HCl (36.5).
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates performed moderately in this question. Most candidates were able to correctly identify the process and gas but struggled to give a reason, whereas others gave the correct reason but identified the wrong gas.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'a', candidates accurately identified the given process as 'diffusion'. In part 'b', they demonstrated clarity in the conceptual understanding of the relationship between molar masses and the rate of diffusion of gases by stating that ammonia has a lower relative molecular mass (17 compared to HCl's 36.5).
questions.weakerResponses: In part 'a', candidates misunderstood the information given in the question, thus mistaking it for sublimation or thermal decomposition rather than diffusion. In part 'b', weaker responses failed to grasp that lighter gases diffuse faster, and ammonia, being less dense with a lower molar mass (17), would diffuse faster than hydrogen chloride (36.5).
suggestions: Conduct the classic glass-tube demonstration of NH3 and HCl diffusion forming a white ring of NH4Cl closer to the HCl end.
Emphasize Graham's law: lower molecular mass corresponds to higher velocity and faster diffusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Process: Diffusion.
b. Faster gas: Ammonia (NH3).
Reason: According to Graham's law of diffusion, the rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass. Ammonia has a lower molar mass (17 g/mol) than hydrogen chloride (36.5 g/mol); being lighter, its molecules travel with greater average speed.

questions.questionText:
When a piece of Mg ribbon is lit, it burns with a dazzling white light. The combination of Mg with oxygen produces a white substance.
a. Identify the element that has the symbol Mg. (1 Mark)
b. Write a balanced chemical equation to show the given chemical reaction. (2 Marks)
c. Which type of bond is formed in the product of this reaction? (1 Mark)
questions.sloText: Describe the physical and chemical properties of sodium, calcium and magnesium with respect to their position on periodic table.
checkingHints: 1 mark for identifying magnesium.
1 mark for correct chemical formulas (Mg, O2, MgO) and 1 mark for balancing: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO.
1 mark for identifying ionic bond.
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates performed well in part 'a' by correctly identifying magnesium. However, weaker responses showed poor conceptual knowledge, failing to write the balanced equation correctly in part 'b'. Similarly, candidates faced challenges in the identification of the type of bond in part 'c'.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'a', candidates correctly identified magnesium. In part 'b', they demonstrated a clear understanding of the reaction by writing the balanced chemical equation as 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. In part 'c', these responses accurately identified the type of bond formed in the product as ionic.
questions.weakerResponses: In part 'b', candidates failed to write the balanced chemical equation, writing unbalanced expressions like Mg + O -> MgO or Mg + O2 -> MgO2. In part 'c', weaker responses incorrectly identified the type of bond as covalent instead of ionic.
suggestions: Emphasize writing diatomic molecular formulas for elemental gases (O2, H2, N2, Cl2).
Differentiate bond types: reaction between electropositive metal (Mg) and electronegative non-metal (O) produces ionic magnesium oxide.
questions.modelAnswer:
a. Element: Magnesium.
b. Balanced chemical equation: 2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s)
c. Bond type: Ionic bond (electrovalent bond).

questions.questionText:
An experiment shows that a compound Y contains 80% carbon and 20% hydrogen by mass. If the relative molecular mass of this compound is 30.07 g/mol, then
i. calculate the empirical formula of the compound Y. (3 Marks)
ii. determine its molecular formula. (3 Marks)
(Note: Atomic mass of C = 12 amu and H = 1 amu)
questions.sloText: Calculate empirical formula using the percentages of elements; (calculate the molecular formula using molecular mass and empirical formula).
checkingHints: 1 mark for calculating moles of C (80/12 = 6.67) and H (20/1 = 20).
1 mark for simplest atomic ratio C:H = 1:3.
1 mark for empirical formula CH3.
1 mark for empirical formula mass = 15 g/mol.
1 mark for calculating n = 30.07 / 15 ≈ 2.
1 mark for molecular formula C2H6.
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates performed well in part 'i' by accurately presenting the necessary steps for calculating empirical and molecular formulae. They used correct formulae to determine the number of moles of each element and indicated the simplest atomic ratios for the empirical formula.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', candidates accurately demonstrated the required steps for calculating empirical and molecular formulae, using correct formulae to find the moles of each element, and indicating the simplest atomic ratios for the empirical formula. In part 'ii', these responses correctly determined the value of 'n' using the appropriate formula and values to derive the molecular formula accurately.
questions.weakerResponses: In part 'i', weaker responses lacked systematic data presentation and value substitutions, often using percentages directly instead of calculating moles. In part 'ii', candidates continued to struggle, calculating incorrect values for 'n', and consequently arriving at the incorrect molecular formula.
suggestions: Require students to use a structured 4-step framework: Mass/Percentage -> Moles -> Simplest Whole-Number Ratio -> Empirical Formula -> Molecular Formula using n = M_m / M_emp.
Provide practice with non-integer division to solidify ratio determination.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Empirical Formula Calculation:
• Moles of Carbon (C) = 80 / 12 = 6.67 mol
• Moles of Hydrogen (H) = 20 / 1 = 20.0 mol
• Atomic ratio (divide by 6.67):
  C : 6.67 / 6.67 = 1
  H : 20.0 / 6.67 = 3
• Empirical formula = CH3

ii. Molecular Formula Determination:
• Empirical formula mass of CH3 = 12 + 3(1) = 15 g/mol
• n = Molecular mass / Empirical formula mass = 30.07 / 15 = 2.004 ≈ 2
• Molecular formula = (CH3) * 2 = C2H6 (Ethane)

questions.questionText:
You have a solution of copper(II) sulphate in water. You want to obtain solid copper(II) sulphate from it.
i. Describe why the technique of filtering copper(II) sulphate solution will not work. (1 Mark)
ii. Which method will you use instead? Give a reason to support your answer. (2 Marks)
iii. Describe how you will obtain solid copper(II) sulphate in THREE steps using the method identified in part ii. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe crystallization and separation techniques for soluble salts;
checkingHints: 1 mark for describing why filtering does not work (homogeneous solution passes through filter).
1 mark for naming crystallisation and 1 mark for stating the correct reason (preserves hydrated crystals without decomposition).
1 mark for writing each step of crystallization (heating to saturation, cooling for crystals, filtering and drying).
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates performed well in part 'i' by correctly describing why filtering cannot be used to separate copper sulphate from water, highlighting that copper sulphate is soluble and not an insoluble solid. However, candidates with weaker responses struggled in parts 'ii' and 'iii'.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', better responses precisely described the reason for not using the filtering technique: it separates insoluble solids from the liquid. Likewise, in part 'ii', candidates successfully identified the process of crystallisation. These responses in part 'iii' also showed accurate and systematically written steps needed for the separation technique, including heating to saturation, cooling for crystallization, and filtering/drying.
questions.weakerResponses: In part 'i', weaker responses exhibited a lack of critical thinking and reasoning skills, failing to link solubility to filter paper porosity. In part 'ii', most candidates correctly identified the method but failed to justify it. In part 'iii', weaker responses provided inaccurate steps, confusing crystallization with boiling to dryness.
suggestions: Differentiate between evaporation to dryness (which yields anhydrous powder or decomposes sensitive salts) and crystallization (which yields hydrated crystalline solids).
Perform hands-on crystallization practicals with copper sulphate in the school laboratory.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Why Filtration Fails:
Filtration separates only insoluble suspended solids. Copper(II) sulphate is completely soluble in water, forming a homogeneous true solution where dissolved ions pass freely through the pores of filter paper.

ii. Alternative Method & Reason:
• Method: Crystallisation.
• Reason: Upon cooling a concentrated saturated solution, pure solid crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4·5H2O) precipitate without thermal decomposition.

iii. Three Steps of Crystallisation:
1. Heat the solution gently in an evaporating dish until it becomes saturated (crystals appear on a cold glass rod).
2. Allow the hot saturated solution to cool slowly at room temperature, allowing copper(II) sulphate crystals to grow.
3. Filter the crystals from the mother liquor, rinse with cold distilled water, and dry them gently between filter papers.

questions.questionText:
Consider the given dot and cross structure of a compound: [:Cl:]- (2,8,8) [Ca]2+ (2,8,8) [:Cl:]- (2,8,8).
With reference to the given dot and cross structure,
i. identify the type of bond that exists in it. (1 Mark)
ii. describe the role of each atom in the formation of the bond identified in part i. (2 Marks)
iii. write any THREE general characteristics of such types of compounds. (3 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the characteristics of ionic compounds; (describe the formation of an ionic bond.)
checkingHints: 1 mark for identifying ionic bond.
1 mark for role of calcium (loses 2 electrons to form Ca2+) and 1 mark for role of chlorine (each Cl gains 1 electron to form Cl-).
1 mark for each valid general characteristic of ionic compounds (any 3 required: high melting/boiling points, electrical conduction in molten/aqueous state, solubility in polar water).
questions.overallPerformance: Overall, candidates performed well in part 'i' by correctly identifying the type of chemical bonding in the given figure as ionic. Weaker responses, however, struggled to identify the type of bond correctly, often predicting covalent bonding. In part 'ii', they failed to explain the correct electron transfer in the formation of ions and lacked knowledge of the characteristics of ionic compounds.
questions.betterResponses: Better responses accurately identified the type of chemical bonding as ionic in part 'i'. In part 'ii', candidates provided a clear description of the electron transfer, forming Ca^2+ and 2Cl^- ions. Similarly, in part 'iii', these responses drafted accurate general characteristics of ionic compounds, such as crystalline structure, electrical conductance, high melting and boiling points, and solubility in polar solvents like water.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses struggled to identify the correct type of bond, often predicting covalent bonding instead of ionic bonding. In part 'ii', candidates failed to describe the appropriate electron transfer for the formation of ions, and their responses mostly revolved around sharing of electrons. Additionally, they lacked knowledge of the characteristics of ionic compounds.
suggestions: Emphasize the distinction between electron transfer (ionic bonding between metal and non-metal) and electron sharing (covalent bonding between non-metals).
Relate physical properties of ionic lattices (high melting point, brittle nature, electrical conductivity in liquid states) to electrostatic attraction.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Bond Type: Ionic bond (electrovalent bond).

ii. Role of Each Atom:
• Calcium atom: Loses its 2 valence electrons to achieve stable octet (2,8,8), becoming a Ca^2+ cation.
• Chlorine atoms: Each of the two chlorine atoms gains 1 electron into its valence shell to achieve stable octet (2,8,8), becoming Cl^- anions.

iii. Three General Characteristics of Ionic Compounds:
1. High melting and boiling points due to strong electrostatic attraction holding the giant ionic lattice together.
2. Good electrical conductors in aqueous solution or molten state where ions are free to move, but non-conductors in solid state.
3. Soluble in polar solvents like water and insoluble in non-polar organic solvents.

questions.questionText:
i. Define the term, ‘electrolysis’. (1 Mark)
ii. Describe the electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine). Support your answer by writing chemical equations for reactions occurring at the cathode and the anode of the electrolytic cell. (5 Marks)
questions.sloText: Describe the manufacturing of sodium hydroxide from aqueous solution of NaCl.
checkingHints: 1 mark for defining electrolysis.
1 mark for reduction of H+ cation and 1 mark for hydrogen gas formation at cathode: 2H+ + 2e- -> H2.
1 mark for oxidation of Cl- anions and 1 mark for chlorine gas formation at anode: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-.
1 mark for combination of Na+ and OH- ions in solution to form sodium hydroxide.
questions.overallPerformance: The candidates' overall performance was assessed, taking note of their responses in defining electrolysis and explaining the stepwise process of electrolysis of concentrated sodium chloride solution (brine). Most candidates drafted the response in an appropriate way and remained successful in defining electrolysis and anodic and cathodic reactions that occur in electrolytic cells. However, a few candidates got confused in the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride.
questions.betterResponses: In part 'i', better responses accurately defined electrolysis as the decomposition of an electrolyte through the passage of electricity or a technique using direct electric current to drive a non-spontaneous chemical reaction. In part 'ii', candidates provided a detailed description of the electrolysis of brine, including the discharge of hydrogen ions at the cathode to form hydrogen gas (2H+ + 2e- -> H2), the discharge of chloride ions at the anode to form chlorine gas (2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-), and the formation of sodium hydroxide solution from sodium ions and hydroxide ions.
questions.weakerResponses: Weaker responses lacked a clear definition of electrolysis. For instance, they wrote 'it is a chemical process by passing an electric current into electrolytic solution' and were unable to describe the stepwise process of electrolysis of brine, rather mentioning the stages of electrolysis of molten sodium chloride via Down's cell. They struggled to describe the discharge of ions at the cathode and anode, as well as the formation of sodium hydroxide solution.
suggestions: Carefully distinguish between Down's cell (electrolysis of molten NaCl yielding liquid sodium and Cl2 gas) and Nelson's / Membrane cell (electrolysis of aqueous brine yielding H2, Cl2, and NaOH solution).
Practice writing half-reactions with state symbols and electron balance.
questions.modelAnswer:
i. Definition of Electrolysis:
Electrolysis is the process of chemical decomposition of an ionic compound (electrolyte) in molten state or aqueous solution into its constituent elements by the passage of a direct electric current.

ii. Electrolysis of Concentrated NaCl (Brine):
• At the Anode (Oxidation):
  Chloride ions (Cl-) are selectively discharged due to their high concentration in brine, releasing electrons to evolve chlorine gas:
  2Cl^-(aq) -> Cl2(g) + 2e^-

• At the Cathode (Reduction):
  Hydrogen ions (H+) from water have a higher reduction potential than Na+ and are discharged at the cathode, gaining electrons to evolve hydrogen gas:
  2H^+(aq) + 2e^- -> H2(g)

• Accumulation in Solution:
  As H+ and Cl- ions leave the solution as gases, the remaining sodium ions (Na+) and hydroxide ions (OH-) combine in the aqueous electrolyte, forming a sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution:
  Na^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) -> NaOH(aq)

• Overall Cell Reaction:
  2NaCl(aq) + 2H2O(l) -> 2NaOH(aq) + Cl2(g) + H2(g)
